summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On December 27, 1997, at approximately 7:45 a.m., a motorist observed a flaming object falling at high speed. The phenomenon was silent and very brief, lasting about three seconds. It was blue-yellow in color. Another witness also reported the same observation. The descriptions given by the witnesses suggest the possibility of atmospheric reentry.

summary: A cloud phenomenon is likely to be observed.
description: On December 14, 1997, around 5:00 PM, a witness in a car spotted a luminous phenomenon he couldn't explain. He had the presence of mind to film the phenomenon, which was probably caused by clouds. After reviewing the video, it was returned to its owner, who intended to use it for commercial purposes.

summary: Observation of bright flashes causing brief power outages
description: On December 11, 1997, at approximately 11:00 PM, silent flashes of light were observed by military personnel. Simultaneously, brief power outages occurred. These outages were confirmed by EDF (the French electricity provider) as being due to an incident on the 33 kV line serving the area. Given the simultaneous occurrence of these events, it is likely that the observed flashes occurred on the 33 kV line at the same time as the incidents reported on that line.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On November 13, 1997, at approximately 7:30 PM, a witness observed a luminous phenomenon moving towards Earth at high speed for a few seconds. The phenomenon was silent and orange in color. The witness's description suggests that this was an atmospheric reentry, which was also observed by other witnesses.

summary: Recovery of a weather balloon.
description: On October 28, 1997, children recovered the remains of a weather balloon from brambles: a ball made of two interlocking aluminum parts attached to a parachute, as well as fragments of balloon also recovered nearby.

summary: Observation of 2 bright objects in the morning sky: probably observation of clouds.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named WORMHOUT (59) 1997, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On October 22, 1997, at approximately 8:22 a.m., a witness, driving to medical appointments, observed a bright, yellowish-white, rectangular glow in the sky. After treating a patient, they both noticed that the object was still there and had moved closer to the house. The patient's husband, without going outside, also saw the object through the window. The witness continued driving and a little further on noticed a second, slightly larger, luminous object. Both objects disappeared at 8:40 AM. This observation may have seemed strange given that several people had observed static luminous objects that nevertheless disappeared. Further examination reveals a significant lack of consistency in these testimonies: - Only T1 is a spontaneous witness. T2 gave a statement to the police who came to her home. T2 said that her husband saw it from inside through the window but didn't move while T1 and T2 were outside watching the UFO. - Significant inconsistencies between witnesses: T1 says she left T2's home three times to look at the UFO, twice with T2 (before and after treatment), while T2 says she did not leave after treatment. T1 describes a rectangular object that did not change shape before arriving at T2's home and during two outings, and then a disc-shaped object during outing Ne3. T2 gives no indication of the shape and only positions himself in relation to T1's earlier statements, saying, "I can't tell you if it's an oval or rectangular object." T2 cites T2's husband as having seen the object move in the sky, while T2 mentions nothing about the movement and T1 says the object was stationary during the first two outings. T2 says he saw the UFO disappear during his outing with T1, while T1 never saw it disappear (it was no longer there, or no longer in the same place or with the same shape, during outing 3). - Little information about its position in the sky. We understand that at 8:25 AM, T1 and T2 were observing the sky together in the direction presumably EAST or SOUTHEAST, as T2 mentions it "in the direction of Esquelbec" (which is at 155°) and T1 indicates a movement of the UFO towards SE in the final phase of observation. We can Note that T2 does not share the strange experience perceived by T1 and only minimally cooperates with his testimony under the request of the police. T1 describes a very bright UFO, white and yellowish in color, and T2 an object that shone like the sun. At 8:25 AM, the sun is in the East (106th parallel) and slightly below the horizon (-1st parallel). It is not yet visible but could brightly illuminate a cloud located to the East or Southeast and stand out against the blue morning sky (T1 describes the UFO in a blue sky). This cloud hypothesis could explain the disappearance of the UFO between T1's second and third appearances, as well as its reappearance (it could also be another cloud) in a changed, disc-shaped form later during appearance 3. The final perception of the oval UFO's movement could stem from T1's own movement by car. It can be established with a high degree of probability that it was a perfectly rectangular shape. and the strong glow of the cloud that misled T1. Regarding T2, this could be interpreted as a form of minimal complicity with T1. In the heat of the moment, T1 drew T2 and her husband into this testimony, which would not have been given spontaneously. The same emotion then led T1 to repeat her mistake with this cloud or another of a different shape. This set of testimonies lies on the border between being unusable due to its weak consistency and a probable explanation (cloud). We adopt the "cloud" explanation due to the absence of any contradictory evidence. GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable cloud observation.

summary: Observation of a luminous object passing over the witnesses' house
description: On October 10, 1999, at approximately 9:15 PM, a couple observed a bright point in the sky from their home. After disappearing for a few moments, the bright point (visible diameter 3 to 4 mm) descended and grew larger as it approached the house. The witnesses then distinguished two rows of eight non-dazzling yellow lights. As it passed over the house, the witnesses perceived a muffled whooshing sound that they were unable to identify as the noise of an airplane. The investigation failed to identify the phenomenon.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On September 29, 1997, at approximately 12:15 PM, a witness in a car observed a fireball with a trail of black smoke for a few moments. The witness's description suggests that the fireball was re-entered into the atmosphere.

summary: Observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On the night of September 23-24, 1997, two independent witnesses observed the passage of a very bright, ovoid-shaped light with a trail. The phenomenon was very rapid and disappeared after a few seconds. No sound was detected. The characteristics of the observation suggest that it was an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Observation of a bright point next to the Moon: mistaken for the planet Jupiter.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as type C, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This particular observation was classified as type C in 1997 by SEPRA. On September 13, 1997, at 10:00 PM, a witness observed a very bright point of light next to the moon from their balcony. The witness filmed the observation and noted that the UFO moved very quickly and appeared to circle the moon. The witness observed the phenomenon again at 10:30 PM, still in the same location. No copy of the video recording was sent to GEIPAN. This case is consistent (a single witness, but the UFO was filming), and the description of the observed UFO is very precise. The witness's sincerity and credibility have never been questioned. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color, position) with a well-known astronomical object: the planet Jupiter. Furthermore, Jupiter was indeed present in the observed area of the sky, to the left of the Moon, although the witness makes no mention of it. The alleged movements of the UFO can be perfectly explained by the camera's movements. It is not the witness's visual perception that is at issue, but rather the witness's interpretation of the observation based on their feelings (astonishment, nighttime observation, interpretation of a video recording). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as PAN A, an observation linked to a misunderstanding with the planet Jupiter.

summary: Probable observation of a celestial body
description: On the evening of September 11, 1997, and again the following day, witnesses reported a bright, twinkling point in the sky. The phenomenon was silent, moving very slowly across the sky, and about the size of a star. It produced a red halo and twinkled with several colors. The observation lasted approximately an hour and a half. This observation was probably of the path of a celestial body.

summary: Three observations over two days and in different directions of a luminous orange ball moving and disappearing: lack of reliable information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and also known as BAGNOLS SUR CEZE 1997, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On Tuesday, September 9, 1997, at 9:30 PM, a witness located on Chemin des Malins in Saint-Gervais (30) observed a luminous sphere rising from the Fontesquiere hill, pausing briefly, varying in brightness, and then disappearing. On Thursday, September 11, at 9:30 PM, the same witness, located on Chemin des Abels in Saint-Gervais (30), observed a sphere above the Cazelle rock. The sphere rose, paused, followed a horizontal trajectory westward, and then disappeared. Half an hour later, at 10:00 PM, the witness (who did not specify their location) again observed a sphere in the hills of Cristolle. This sphere rose from the ground and disappeared. For each observation, the witness described a luminous orange sphere with an apparent diameter of 8 to 10 centimeters. No other reports were collected. No traces were found on the ground. The atmospheric conditions reported by the gendarmerie were very good (a very clear and starry night with no wind). The gendarmerie investigation indicates that the night of September 9th was illuminated by the fireworks display in the town of Bagnols-sur-Cèze, concluding a local festival. The witness made no distinction in the appearance of the unidentified flying object (UFO) between his three observations (September 9th at 10:00 PM, September 11th at 9:30 PM and 10:00 PM). Four hypotheses are being considered: a child's balloon that escaped, a tethered balloon that escaped, a Thai lantern, or aircraft (see the investigation report). The backscattering of urban streetlights is thought to explain the luminous nature of these balloons. The festive nature of these balloons, especially a tethered balloon several meters in diameter, is only compatible with the observation of September 9th (the closing night of the village festival). This balloon hypothesis cannot apply to September 11th, particularly since the areas overflown are less conducive to backlighting from the ground. The hypotheses to consider are therefore: - an aircraft or lantern on September 11th; - an aircraft, lantern, child's balloon, or tethered balloon on September 9th. Considering that the witness would have reported any difference in appearance had they perceived them during the different observations, it is estimated that the probability that they would have noted no difference in appearance between these four hypotheses of such different natures (especially if the balloon type is only possible the first time) is zero. Therefore, the goal is to find a common hypothesis for the observations, between a lantern and an aircraft. Note that if we were to limit ourselves to the observation of September 9th, the child's balloon hypothesis would also be eliminated. The backscattering of ground lights cannot explain the perception of a ball for a child's balloon seen from such a distance on September 9th. This difficulty in explanation is less pronounced for a captive balloon that escaped, as it is larger, but its probability of presence is lower on a holiday and even lower on any other day. The aircraft hypothesis could only correspond to a light or military aircraft, or a helicopter, to be so low and so close, but the single (and orange) light is completely incompatible (incompatibility with the UFO's trajectory, absence of anti-collision lights) for just one of the observations, let alone for all three. The release of Thai lanterns appears, in terms of appearance and trajectory, consistent with the first two observations (September 9th and 11th) and the little-known details of the last one on September 11th. The skepticism surrounding this hypothesis stems primarily from the fact that Thai lanterns were rare in France in 1997 and only became popular around 2005 or 2007. However, tourists who had purchased them during their summer travels in Asia may have wanted to create a sensation with them at the first festival upon their return. The pioneering and sensational nature of this festive practice on September 9th could then have encouraged its repetition on the next favorable evening (September 11th), for the enjoyment of the initiator and a few spectators already impressed or enticed by the discovery on September 9th. Regarding the consistency of the account, there is only one witness, but they provide a fairly precise description of the locations and trajectories, except for the third observation. Regarding the three successive sightings, it is regrettable that the gendarmerie did not explicitly describe each of the three observations in order to encourage the expression of any potential differences in perception. The lantern hypothesis may fit the descriptions, but its probability is diminished by their still rare use in 1997. The repetition two days later, outside of a festive evening, leads to additional hypotheses, certainly plausible (the temptation to repeat such a novel experiment as soon as possible), but still reducing the probability. Ultimately, the evidence proves too marginal to support such a hypothesis, even though it remains conceivable. These two factors also preclude maintaining the case in the "Unidentified Aerial Phenomenon" category. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies it as category C and concludes: lack of reliable information.

summary: Observation of the very slow passage of a very large triangular object: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named PARIS (75) 1997, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On September 7, 1997, at 1:43 AM, a witness observed from their balcony a large triangular shape with two blue lights and one green light moving slowly along a straight path. The observation lasted 12 seconds. No noise was heard, but the witness felt vibrations in his body, and when he tried to take a picture, his camera jammed. Only one witness statement was collected. This statement describes numerous strange occurrences which, taken at face value, led the GEIPAN (SEPRA) at the time to classify the case as unexplained. This new examination does not confirm this classification. Indeed, the testimony lacks sufficient consistency, especially in terms of reliability, to validate its strange nature and is therefore unusable. The (unexplainable) elements of strangeness are numerous and significant, but they present strong differences and inconsistencies depending on the source: the police report from the day after the sighting, and the witness's publication three months later, which he submitted to the police. The witness is the editor-in-chief of a magazine called "Strangeness and Mysteries" and published his observation in his own magazine. It's worth noting that he therefore has an interest in his journal in having testimonies that introduce an element of mystery. But we will first consider the inconsistencies between the two accounts of the observation: - the triggering of the observation. In one case (report), the triggering is visual; the witness first sees the triangle, observes it through binoculars and a camera, then feels vibrations in his body and on the windows. In the other (publication), the strange occurrence begins with vibrations, not of the windows, but of numerous plants on the balcony, with details of their synchronicity with the vibrations in his body, then he sees the triangle in the sky. It is surprising that the witness doesn't know exactly what triggered the strange occurrence, just as it is surprising that what is a priori the strangest thing (the vibrations in the absence of noise) involves such different elements (windows, plants). It should be noted that the temporal inconsistency is already present between the two interviews with the police (at the station and at home). - Duration: 12 seconds in one case and more than 17 seconds in the other, where it is stated that this was measured with a stopwatch. Why is the stopwatch mentioned 3 months later to produce different information? - Angular size: the PAN (Phantom Angle of Motion) is covered by 3 fingers in one case, 4 in the other. - Camera: in one case, the witness reports the camera's inability to capture the image and simply states (without indicating anything unusual) that no picture was taken. But 3 months later, a genuine oddity emerges: the camera refuses to take the picture when the shutter button is pressed, even after switching to manual focus. These are sufficient elements to question the reliability of a single human testimony without any photographic or other evidence, especially since such a level of reported strangeness requires (GEIPAN methodology) a very high level of reliability to characterize the observation as unexplained. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as C: unusable testimony. The fact that the witness published their testimony in their own magazine on mystery and the strange, and that they expressed their conviction regarding the reality of the strange occurrences and the conspiracy to conceal this reality, also constitutes a further element to question its reliability (although the observed inconsistencies are already sufficient to conclude that it is reliable). Indeed, the witness's testimony serves the interests of their magazine and reflects the positions and convictions they or the magazine espouse.

summary: Observing the Moon under special conditions
description: On September 7, 1997, around 2 a.m., a couple watching fireworks observed a stationary luminous phenomenon to the right of the display. Simultaneously, in another town, another couple made the same observation. One of the witnesses filmed the phenomenon, which appeared to be very close, about ten meters above the ground. The investigation conducted jointly by the gendarmerie and the SEPRA (Scientific and Technical Observatory of the Moon) unambiguously demonstrated that the observed phenomenon was the moon under specific conditions (cloudy skies and the beginning of an eclipse).

summary: Observation of circles of light rotating on themselves, probably originating from an advertising laser projector
description: On the night of August 29-30, 1997, around midnight, several witnesses were alerted by the unusual behavior of farm animals. Upon arriving at the farm, they observed a white, round glow, with an outer hoop and an inner hoop studded with small luminous circles, projecting beams of light towards the ground. The entire object moved while rotating on its axis. At 2:00 AM, as the witnesses were going to bed, the phenomenon was still present. Although no evidence from the investigation confirmed it, it appears that this observation was the reflection on the clouds of an advertising laser projector capable of operating within a radius of 8 to 10 km.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On August 27, 1997, at approximately 4:45 a.m., several witnesses across the Lorraine region observed a very rapid passage of a green sphere across the sky with a yellow-orange trail. The silent phenomenon lasted 2 to 3 seconds. The characteristics of these accounts are consistent with the probable observation of an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of a low-altitude flying object shining a spotlight on the witnesses: observation of a helicopter.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named LYON (69) 1997, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On August 27, 1997, at approximately 9:45 PM, three witnesses returning from work observed a triangular object (or rather, round, according to the witnesses) moving silently at low altitude and in complete silence. The craft was equipped with two large lights. Upon approaching the witnesses, one of the spotlights was briefly shone on them. Two figures inside a glass-enclosed compartment were seen by one of the witnesses. The gendarmerie received a letter from T1, co-signed by T2 and T3, and interviewed the three witnesses. The official report states that: - T1: The aircraft was above the helicopter landing and maneuvering area of the hospital. T1's suspicions lay in the momentary shining of the spotlight towards her on the ground, the absence of noise, and the fact that she did not see the propeller or the exhaust system. - T2 reiterated T1's first two suspicions but also saw green and red lights characteristic of aviation navigation lights. - T3 does not specify any particular strangeness ("I didn't pay much attention to this phenomenon and I returned to my vehicle"). This occurred in an area where helicopters are present and land. Everything described is consistent with a helicopter flight. The witnesses are, however, presumably familiar with helicopters because they work at the hospital. The absence of noise led GEIPAN at the time to dismiss this hypothesis. But since then, there have been many other cases where witnesses do not perceive the noise of a helicopter at 100 or 200 meters, so focused is their perceptual attention on the visual and/or emotional factors. We also know that the noise depends on wind conditions. See on www.geipan.fr the cases of MESSINCOURT (08) 10.03.1994 or [D417] of MUNSTER (68) around COLMAR (68) 13.11.2015. What triggered the strangeness for the witnesses, especially for T1 who may have influenced T2 (T3 seems uninvolved) by shouting about a UFO, was the spotlight being pointed at them. Helicopters, however, quite often point spotlights at the ground. Other reported strange elements, such as the lack of sightings of propellers or a gas exhaust system, are not to be considered given the nighttime conditions of observation. On the other hand, the green and red lights and the slow speed of movement strengthen the helicopter hypothesis. The overall testimonies are rather inconsistent. It seems that T1 may have influenced T2 and T3, who do not express the same perception of strangeness. It is imprecise and leads to inconsistencies (regarding the lights, for example). The helicopter hypothesis leaves little doubt, mainly due to the location, the Green and red lights, references to this hypothesis by witnesses, and the explanation of the phenomena triggering the strangeness (the spotlight shining and the absence of noise). Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: helicopter.

summary: Observation of luminous spheres rotating in the sky: probable laser effects.
description: On August 27, 1997, at approximately 11:00 PM, a witness observed six luminous orbs rotating in the sky. After a while, five of the spheres disappeared, leaving behind a large, milky sphere (three times the size of the setting sun) which he observed for about half an hour. The witness then called his mother, who only observed the large white sphere. Although the investigation did not prove it, the described observation is reminiscent of the effects produced on clouds by advertising laser projectors.

summary: Observation of two objects in the Parisian sky: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named PARIS (75) 1997, is part of a set of cases recently re-examined. On Sunday, August 24, 1997, at 8:01 PM, a witness observed and photographed two UFOs (Unidentified Flying Objects) over Paris (75). He contacted a scientific journal, which advised him to inform the DGAC (French Civil Aviation Authority). The latter contacted the headquarters of the Air Transport Gendarmerie, which instructed the Paris Air Transport Gendarmerie Brigade (BGTA) to launch an investigation. On September 4, 1997, Gendarmerie investigators went to the witness's home to interview him and view the nine slides he had had made at a private laboratory. Eight of these nine slides were then sent successively to the Gendarmerie's central photographic laboratory, and then to the Gendarmerie's criminal research institute. A further interview with the witness was conducted by the gendarmes on October 11, 1997, to gather more information. At that time, the witness also made a sketch of the aircraft carrier, which was given to the gendarmes. Finally, a study was conducted by SEPRA in May 1998, followed by an exchange of letters and faxes between the witness, SEPRA, and the company Fleximage; the latter receiving a detailed account of the witness's observation in June 1998. The case was subsequently classified as Category D by SEPRA, due to the difficulty in disentangling and clarifying the various elements of strangeness among: 1) What was seen by the witness; 2) What was on the slides presented to the police; 3) What was found on a new printout once the slides had been cleaned of developing residue; and 4) What the witness said about the UFO after reviewing the printout. It is now established that: Point 2): the UFO seen by the witness is not on the slides presented to the police. They are alerted by a spot on the photos (boomerang-shaped) which turns out to be a residue of developing product. Point 3): a printout from one of the cleaned slides fortuitously contains an artifact (since nothing equivalent exists on the slide) in the shape of a hollow pentahedron. Point 4): the printout is presented to the witness without revealing the artifactual nature of the object. The witness, asked to comment on this object, does not make the connection with the observed UFO. However, the witness subsequently gives new accounts of their testimony: the UFO initially described (and drawn) as resembling a greasy piece of paper carried by the wind with jagged edges becomes: Its remarkable shape against the blue background of the sky was extraordinary: five sides, a pentahedron. We therefore know that the UFO observed by the witness is not on the slides and also that the witness was subsequently influenced, consciously or unconsciously (false memory phenomenon), by what he saw on the printed image. Point 1): The absence of the object on the slide does not cast doubt on the witness's initial description. However, no information is available (or unambiguously usable) concerning the angular dimensions or the angular height above the horizon of the UFO. For example, an altitude of 5000m is meaningless since a witness cannot judge the distance of an unknown object. During their visit to the witness's home, the investigators focused on viewing the slides without conducting further investigations (photographs of the locations where the images were taken, angular measurements from the observation window). Nevertheless, the limited information available is consistent with the observation of a light object (debris, paper, balloon) carried by the wind, as the wind (weather data) was blowing in the direction of the observed movement of the UFO. In conclusion, we have a series of usable photographs, but careful analysis does not reveal the presence of any UFO, and we lack sufficient information to identify the UFO described by the witness. However, the description does not suggest anything particularly strange, as it is consistent with a light object carried by the wind. Consequently, GEIPAN reclassifies the case as eCe: Unusable testimony due to lack of reliable information.

summary: Long-term observations of a luminous phenomenon seemingly following one of the witnesses on his journey in a vehicle: an astronomical misinterpretation of Jupiter.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This particular case is classified as D and was previously named SAINT-ANDRE (974) 1997. On August 15, 1997, around 5:00 a.m., a street vendor (T1) making his rounds in the town of Saint-André observed a stationary luminous object about forty meters above the ground. He later noticed that the phenomenon was following him and became frightened. Upon arriving in Bras-Panon, he woke his sister (T2) and his family, and they all witnessed the presence of the UFO. Since then, T2 says he regularly observes the UFO when the weather is clear, but much further away. T1 provides no information on the UFO's position; this can only be deduced from T2's statement. The described phenomenon strongly suggests the observation of an astronomical object. Indeed: - for T1, we note the characteristics of a "following UFO" (a perceptual illusion due to the witness's own movement, when the UFO's origin is very far away, as in the case of a celestial body). In fact, the UFO seems to stop when the witness is stationary and resume its course when they move again. This perception generates strong emotions (perhaps with the idea or hypothesis of encountering an intelligent being). - For T2, we note that the UAP is in the same place in the sky at the same time for several days. What is described also includes strange features that might seem to contradict the hypothesis of a celestial body: T1 perceives the UAP (at least at the start of its observation) in a shape "almost like a turtle", "with headlights". T2's perception is different and less strange: "My brother came to wake me up around five or five thirty, and he told us to look in the sky, there is a big light. He told us that he had seen it up close, that it had passed over his head. He was very scared when he arrived home. My husband, my son and I looked in the direction he was pointing to (Salazie) and we observed for a very long time, a very bright light, sometimes it moved to the right, sometimes to the left, the light was sometimes very strong and sometimes it weakened." However, T1 is quite certain that T2 and his family observed the UFO, as he says: "I told them what I had just seen, and they went outside with me, accompanied by their seventeen-year-old son, to observe the object. They all saw it; it didn't move. The shape was a little difficult to discern, but the two lights were very visible. We stayed and observed it until 5:50 a.m., at which time I left to continue my rounds. The craft never moved. The rest of the family stayed and observed until the craft disappeared. They told me that it suddenly plunged behind one of the many cliffs in the Salazie area." For T2, what distinguishes the UFO from a star is this: "It's much too big; when you look at it, there are rays around it," plus possibly the movement described above. But T2 also specifies this: "Since that date, the mysterious thing is always there, when the weather is fine. Around 6:30 or 6:30 PM, when night falls, we see the bright phenomenon. It is always in the same place, and we observe small colored lights (red, green, orange) that seem to leave the sphere or come from that direction and head towards the sea, and then we can't see it anymore. We see this thing very high in the sky and we can't distinguish exactly what it is. When T1 came to wake us up, we looked at the phenomenon; it was at the same height as we see it on other days. I couldn't draw it; I think with binoculars we would have a better chance of seeing it and distinguishing what the object is made of." What T2 describes, as being present every day at 6:30 PM and then disappearing, is like the 5 AM UAP ("the mysterious thing is always there") and therefore located to the west (T2 describes the 5 AM UAP "in the direction of Salazie," which is west at azimuth 250° from T2's location). It is unequivocally Venus, which does indeed become visible at 6:30 PM low on the horizon before setting. T2's misidentification of Venus is quite common (see www.geipan.fr, search for cases using the keyword "Venus"), often caused, as here, by the strong brightness and changing colors (through light rays from the low-elevation atmosphere). The UAP seen by T2 and T1 at 5 AM on August 15th is described by T2 as being present in the evening at 6:30 PM. And indeed, at 5 AM, in the same place in the sky as Venus at 6:30 PM, there is Jupiter (barely 20 arcseconds apart, with a similar elevation of around 20 arcseconds), and Jupiter shines brighter than all the stars, almost as bright as Venus (magnitude -2.8 versus magnitude -3.9), and can exhibit the same changing light patterns (see the reconstruction document). The UFO seen by T1 and T2 at 5 AM is therefore, without a doubt, Jupiter. The other peculiarity described by T2, slight movements of the UFO, is a well-known perceptual phenomenon called autokinetic (see the article on the autokinetic effect). The striking strangeness described by T1 (turtle with headlights) lacks a definitive objective explanation, though it doesn't call into question the Jupiter hypothesis given the coincidence of other elements. T1 indicates that during the joint observation with T2, the shape was difficult to discern but that "the two headlights were very clearly visible," whereas T2 only describes a dazzling light whose glow was strong or could dim. There may have been cloud cover, which, for T2, caused the variation in the glow and, for T1, resulted in a blurred and variable shape (perhaps less so during the first observation) around the glow. The double glow seen by T1 could result from an optical aberration caused by eyeglasses (it is unknown whether the witness wore them). This aberration is typically caused by vehicle windows and windshields, which could have been at play during the first phase of observation and also solidified the memory in the second phase, assuming the eyeglasses were not the cause in both phases. T1's intense fear (probably linked to the illusion of the following ball) and described by T2 ("he was very scared when he got home") could have altered the quality of perception and activated interpretive mechanisms (vehicle, headlights). This observation is interesting for several reasons: - the strangeness that can arise from observing a very bright celestial body due to the physical or human phenomena that can be involved (color distortion caused by the atmosphere, shapes created by cloud cover, autokinetic effects, the illusion of a following sphere, etc.). - differences in perceptions and the sense of strangeness experienced by different witnesses for the same observation. - the possible effect of contagion of strangeness. It is likely that T2 found what was seen every evening at 6:30 PM even stranger after the alert created by his brother with the 5:00 AM UFO sighting. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: observation of Jupiter.

summary: Observation of the slow passage of a point of light
description: On August 9, 1997, at approximately 10:40 PM, a witness observing the sky with his nephew was intrigued by the passage of a very bright, slowly moving point of light. The observation lasted approximately 30 to 40 seconds. There was no sound. We have limited information, but we can assume that the witness likely saw the passage of an aircraft or a satellite.

summary: Observing the passage of light above the trees
description: On August 4, 1997, at approximately 10:00 PM, a witness having dinner observed a yellow light moving above the trees. This light formed three arcs. No further information is available.

summary: Observation of the evolution of whitish oval shapes in the cloudy sky: probable observation of a light animation of skytracer.
description: Recent testimony (March 7, 2013) of an old sighting, the exact date of which the witness does not remember (an arbitrary date is given). The sighting took place on a road between La Rochelle (17) and Niort (79), at the entrance to Niort and then in Échiré (79). One Saturday evening around midnight at the end of August 1997, a motorist and his passengers were surprised to see in the cloudy sky a whitish oval mass around which smaller oval shapes were swirling. No unusual noise was heard. The sighting lasted several hours from different locations, including the witness's home, where he took several photographs with a disposable camera. The witness eventually went to bed. All the photographs are black. Only one testimony has been collected to date. This case of observation of "spinning saucers" in a cloudy sky on a Saturday night for a long time has all the characteristics of skytracers, those projectors used by nightclubs to signal themselves: - fairly typical shape (set of ovoid masses arranged in circles or ellipses). - Typical behavior (continuous rotation around a central point and overall movement by slow sweeping or total or partial rotation, with possible stops). A central beam around which various smaller projectors rotate. - Cloudy sky: ideal surface for the projectors, which trace more or less rounded shapes depending on the angle of incidence and the cloud topography. - And if there is no haze, which is likely in this summer season, the upward beams remain invisible. - It is a Saturday night (the day with the highest frequency for sky tracers) and the summer holiday period, therefore more festive than usual. - The duration is several hours: dance clubs turn on their sky tracers around 10 p.m., until the early morning. - Sky tracers were very fashionable in those years. - No noise heard. - Whitish color: the most frequent for sky tracers. - Large angular size of the whole. - The phenomenon is visible from several tens of kilometers away, and the halos travel over several kilometers. Compatible with the movement of witnesses. - Failed photograph: this is quite normal because the phenomenon is mobile and ultimately not very bright; a camera with a large lens and very sensitive film would have been needed to get a good image of the phenomenon. GEIPAN classifies this case as "B": very probable observation of a "skytracer". The imprecision regarding the date and the age of the event prevents GEIPAN from tracing the precise origin of this projector. See: light animation and light animation

summary: Successive observation of the rapid and silent movement of two phenomena of different shapes in the clear sky: lack of information and cross-checks.
description: Recent testimony (February 23, 2015) of past observations. GEIPAN is processing the observation made in Port-La-Nouvelle (11). On August 4 or 5, 1997, at 11:45 PM (the witness no longer remembers the exact date), two people lying on deck chairs were surprised to see two luminous phenomena appear in the clear sky 10 minutes apart. The first phenomenon is described as flashing orange spots outlining an equilateral triangle. The observation lasted 3 seconds. The silent movement of this UFO from NNE to SSW was very rapid. The second phenomenon is described as two perfectly rectangular yellow/orange lights moving on the same trajectory as the first UFO. The lights moved in parallel and at a short distance from each other. Only one testimony has been collected. The first observation, a dark triangle bordered by three orange lights flying at low altitude, requires interpretation according to the psychology of perception: the witness certainly saw the three orange lights, but the materiality of the triangle is by no means certain, and is very likely the result of a well-known illusion, called a contour illusion or shape illusion (see Psychology of Form). The witness even wrote, "triangle of equilateral shape, seemingly immaterial." On the other hand, the distance estimate, and therefore the speed estimate, has no chance of being accurate since the witness has never seen this phenomenon, which he nevertheless compares to aircraft he has seen (see Estimating the size and distance of an unknown phenomenon). What the witness objectively saw was a set of three bright points crossing half the sky together in three seconds, at an undetermined altitude, from the NNE to the SSW. Two other lights followed the same trajectory 10 minutes later. These could be luminous objects carried by the wind: since the date of the observation is approximate, it is difficult to know the weather conditions that day, and in particular to correlate the movement of these lights with the wind direction. On August 4th, there was a light wind in Perpignan. From E to NE, which cannot explain the observed movement. Due to the unknown date and the impossibility of conducting an investigation more than 17 years after the events, GEIPAN classifies this case as "C" due to a lack of precise date and insufficient corroboration.

summary: Observations of movement with a muffled noise of a dark craft with lights flying over a house: probable sightings of an airplane.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named CHOLET (49) 1997, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On July 21, 1997, between 10:45 PM and 11:15 PM, two witnesses observed, for three or four minutes, a dark object with colored lights on either side and emitting a muffled noise passing over their house from southwest to northeast. Our analysis has shown that the witnesses likely observed, under difficult conditions (during twilight and/or night), a small private plane preparing to land, with its landing lights on, after a night VFR/IMC flight, possibly at Ancenis airport (see the investigation report). The noise perceived, similar to that of a small plane according to T1, as well as the total duration of the observation, perfectly fits the hypothesis. The precise shape of the aircraft is difficult to discern against the already very dark sky (see the astronomical situation). The witnesses describe a circular object, elongated in length and wingless, but this is most certainly a classic perceptual illusion, the brain unconsciously attempting to reconstruct a solid shape, as the UFO is only visible through its lights. The arrangement of the lights, as described by the witnesses, is also entirely consistent with the observation of an aircraft approaching head-on. The observation began when the aircraft was low enough on the horizon for the perspective to compress into the triangular shape defined by the three landing lights (one at the front and the other two further back), so that they appeared horizontally aligned or nearly so. The testimonies, however, diverge on the color of the lights, described as white by T2 and red by T1. But T1 only observed the final phase, which only allowed the landing lights to be seen obliquely to the beams and at a much lower intensity, often perceived as reddish while still retaining a white dominance. Another discrepancy is that at the moment T1 saw these lights as red, T2 no longer saw any light. One explanation, besides the possibility of one of the two witnesses failing to remember the information, could be that the difference in visual acuity prevented T2 from distinguishing (or at least retaining) what T1 could still see. More difficult to explain is the lack of visibility of the anti-collision lights in this final phase when the aircraft passes directly over (or almost directly over) the witnesses. While at the beginning of the observation, these lights may be obscured by the bright landing lights, as the angle of observation increases with the aircraft's approach to the witnesses, the anti-collision lights should be visible, no longer obscured by the landing lights, which are themselves less visible due to the angle of observation. Was this a deliberate (and dangerous) maneuver by the pilot, who might have switched them off in unsuitable weather conditions? The confirmed presence of some clouds at an altitude of 1500 meters could, however, explain this likely temporary extinguishing of the anti-collision lights during an IMC flight of this aircraft. This, however, requires qualification, as it seems surprising that the witnesses never mentioned observing the aircraft pass through a cloud, especially given that the moon was full and could have illuminated them, making them visible against the dark sky. This last point, however, does not appear sufficient to rule out the hypothesis, as it is not without possible explanation and given the importance of the other points supporting it. The consistency of the evidence is moderate. We have two eyewitness accounts, one of which is particularly detailed, but it lacks data useful for analysis, such as angular measurements (dimensions of the UFO, altitude above the horizon during the different phases, etc.). Above all, there are contradictions between witnesses that the police investigation has not attempted to qualify or quantify. The evidence is barely sufficient to validate the airplane hypothesis with its residual element of strangeness (the airplane hypothesis must be linked to specific aeronautical, atmospheric, or visibility circumstances). The case is classified as Class B, bordering on unusable due to a lack of consistency (level and reliability of the information).

summary: Observation of two successive luminous phenomena by the crew of a sailboat
description: In the early hours of July 4, 1997, at 4:00 AM, a witness at the helm of his sailboat observed an intense glow that descended rapidly for 2 to 3 seconds, stabilized for a few moments, then quickly moved horizontally and disappeared in approximately 2 or 3 seconds. The witness called his two crewmates, who were asleep, to report his observation when they witnessed a second phenomenon: a yellow-ochre diamond shape with lights at its points. The object moved very quickly at cloud level and disappeared after 10 to 15 seconds. The observed phenomena remain unexplained.

summary: Very long observation of an ovoid and silent UFO flying at low altitude over a car; indirect testimony: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive. Among its publications are older cases, originally classified as type A to D, which are now being re-examined. The aim of this re-examination is not to lower or raise any particular classification category, but rather to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This observation is one of these re-examined cases. On June 23, 2007, a resident of Béziers (34) reported to the gendarmerie that his son and daughter-in-law had observed a UFO for an extended period on the night of June 21, 1997, around midnight. While traveling on the N609 from Béziers, the driver and his passenger observed a flattened, ovoid-shaped object for 45 minutes; non-luminous white lights emanated from it. Throughout the journey, the unidentified flying object (UFO) hovered above the vehicle, which it appeared to be following. According to the passenger, the UFO appeared and disappeared regularly. The witnesses heard no unusual noises. The UFO was approximately 50 meters above the ground. No other witness statements were collected regarding this phenomenon. The investigation conducted by the gendarmerie failed to identify an aircraft that could correspond to this observation. Furthermore, the two direct witnesses, residents of the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence department (04), could not be interviewed as they had returned home by the time the investigation began. Since the two witnesses could not be interviewed, there is no direct testimony available to re-examine the case. It is reported only by a third party who saw nothing. The case is therefore very weak because it lacks direct testimony. Consequently, in the current GEIPAN classification, this case is classified as PAN C due to a lack of information (total absence of direct testimony).

summary: Observation of two luminous balls moving at high speed
description: On June 6, 1997, around 11 p.m., a witness in his garden observed a stationary luminous sphere, approximately four times smaller than the moon. After a few minutes, a second sphere arrived at very high speed next to the first, and the entire system then moved off at high speed towards the north. The witness called his friend, who was able to observe the departure of both spheres. The police apparently received other calls about this unexplained phenomenon.

summary: Observation of luminous features
description: On May 15 or 25, 1997 (date uncertain), a witness observed luminous "lines" with a small trail in two different locations for a few seconds. No other information is available.

summary: Observation of the rapid passage of a round, luminous shape
description: On May 3, 1997, at approximately 1:30 a.m., a couple returning home from work observed a point of light brighter than the stars in the sky. This point was approaching at high speed, and the witnesses were able to observe a large, rather round, luminous mass that passed directly over the housing development and disappeared to the south. A sound of air movement was heard as the phenomenon passed. The total duration of the observation was approximately 5 minutes. No explanation could be found for this phenomenon.

summary: Observation of the passage of a bright point in the sky: lack of information.
description: Recent report (May 28, 2009) of an earlier observation (April 25, 1997). A witness observed from their office the movement of a large, iridescent yellow light. The observation lasted 20 to 25 minutes. No other reports have been collected about this phenomenon. The description of this light moving slowly in a straight line from south to north suggests a high-altitude balloon. Météo-France reported "light wind from the southwest" that day, which is not entirely consistent with the observation. If it is a scientific balloon, it is unclear where it could have come from (perhaps Italy?). Although the observation is very similar to that of a balloon, GEIPAN lacks sufficient evidence to either confirm or refute this hypothesis. Given the age of the case and its relative lack of unusualness, this case is classified as "C": insufficient information.

summary: Observation of a very bright white glow in the sky accompanied by a firework sound and a partial car fire: fire from a ground rocket.
description: On the night of April 10-11, 1997, a witness was awakened by a very bright white flash followed by the sound of fireworks. Going to the window, he saw that the roof of his car, parked in his driveway, was on fire. The witness immediately called the police. Police and firefighters arrived at the scene to collect samples. The University of Savoie laboratory, which examined the samples, identified basalt and indicated that it was likely a meteorite. A specialist who rushed to the site the next day expressed strong doubts about this hypothesis. Furthermore, an official from the mineralogy laboratory of the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, having examined some debris, also ruled out the possibility of a meteorite impact. The SEPRA (French Society for the Study and Protection of the Environment) was alerted and was able to collect three samples for analysis from the Bioinformatics Laboratory in Tours (see attached document). Further analyses conducted by the CNRS central laboratory in Solaize demonstrated that the samples contained components (sodium, magnesium, potassium, sulfur, and carbon) generally found in the composition of marine or terrestrial rockets (see the AFP dispatch of April 29, 1997, sent to SEPRA): these latter analyses definitively ruled out the hypothesis of a meteorite impact. GEIPAN classified this case as A: vehicle fire caused by a terrestrial rocket. The owner of the partially burned vehicle filed a police report. However, the report was not sent to SEPRA. Currently, without direct testimony and without access to the witness, GEIPAN is not conducting an investigation. We are nevertheless publishing this case because significant work has been carried out and has led to a conclusion. This case also indicates that direct access to the witness would very likely have allowed for better channeling and optimization of investigative efforts.

summary: Observation of several rows of lights
description: On March 24, 1997, at approximately 6:30 a.m., a witness driving his car observed a luminous phenomenon consisting of several superimposed rows of lights over a considerable width, on the order of 200 to 300 meters. The phenomenon was not very fast and moved silently. Its estimated altitude was around 2000 meters, and it was located about 4 kilometers from the witness. No explanation could be found for this observation.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On March 17, 1997, at approximately 9:00 AM, several witnesses, including a TAT flight crew and a Mirage 2000 pilot on a training flight, observed the very rapid passage of a luminous phenomenon descending very quickly. The phenomenon was also observed by three witnesses in the same terms from two villages in the Pyrénées-Orientales. The witnesses' descriptions correspond to the probable observation of an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On March 11, 1997, at approximately 9:30 p.m., two gendarmes on a surveillance mission observed the fall of an incandescent object. The observation was very brief (5 seconds) and silent. The description provided suggests it was likely an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Observation of an object the size of a small pea zigzagging across the sky with a trail
description: On March 9, 1997, between 5:00 and 5:30 AM, a witness observed a zigzagging object, about the size of a pea, with a white trail. The object then stabilized. No further information is available.

summary: Observation of a bright red light with many bright points
description: On March 7, 1997, around midnight, a witness observed a bright light forming a red circle with hundreds of spotlights and moving rapidly. The phenomenon remained silent. No further information could be gathered.

summary: Observation of evolving light patterns
description: On February 13, 1997, a pilot, who was also a helicopter pilot, observed a slowly moving amber-colored streak in the sky. The movement then became very rapid and zigzagged, and a second streak joined the first. The two then moved together. The investigation failed to identify the phenomenon as an aircraft or the reflection of a laser projector. The observation remains unexplained.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of a luminous orange ball in the sky: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. Among its publications are older cases, originally classified as type D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This case, formerly known as VOUZIERS (08) 1997, is classified as type D by SEPRA. On February 19, 1997, the newspaper L'Union published an article recounting a UFO sighting by a resident of VOUZIERS (08) a few days earlier. The local gendarmerie brigade was alerted to this article. The witness was interviewed on February 21st. He reported that while driving his van, he intermittently saw a luminous orange ball moving from west to east across the sky. With the window open, no noise was heard. The investigation conducted on-site in the following days failed to identify any other witnesses or provide any information regarding the UFO sighting. This case is rather weak: - only one witness, inconsistencies between the statements given to the journalist and the police, - lack of precision or consistency regarding the UFO's position in the sky, its duration, and its date. It is possible (through cross-referencing) to resolve some of the inconsistencies or inaccuracies. What can be reconstructed of the sighting reveals many common characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color, trajectory) with a well-known spacecraft: the Mir space station. Furthermore, Mir did indeed make several passes across the sky in the evening during the observation period, under conditions consistent with what can be reconstructed from the observation. However, the MIR hypothesis would correspond to an observation not on February 6th, but on February 5th or 7th, which would remain consistent with the witness testimony since the latter leaves some doubt about the exact date: the witness mentions in the press article "from" to Thursday, February 6th, while in the police report, he mentions "from" to Tuesday, February 6th, 1997. February 6th, 1997 was in fact a Thursday. On February 6th, the station was visible under the observation conditions, but 45 minutes later than the reported time of the observation. It is possible that the witness's error concerns the day rather than the time, although the reverse cannot be ruled out. It is noted that the testimony was given 15 days after the sighting. Overall, the UFO sighting presents numerous similarities with the visibility of the Mir space station during that period. Nevertheless, the inaccuracies or inconsistencies in the testimony (date, UFO's departure direction, the witness's exact position) prevent us from formally identifying this case as a case of mistaken identity with the Mir space station. Conversely, this same inconsistency does not allow us to consider this sighting unexplained. Depending on whether or not we accept the date error, we can conclude: - that it was a sighting of Mir on February 6th (but with a probability barely greater than 0.5) and the conclusion would be UFO sighting MIR. - or that we don't know what the witness saw without having consistent evidence to conduct an investigation or to corroborate a strange observation, and the conclusion would be UAP C: lack of reliable information. GEIPAN chooses the second option and classifies the case as UAP C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Probable observations of a meteorite fall.
description: On February 4, 1997, at approximately 6:20 PM, about ten witnesses spread across several departments in southwestern France observed, for a few seconds, the very rapid passage of a luminous sphere on a descending trajectory with a significant trail. Some witnesses observed the sphere exploding into several pieces. This was undoubtedly an atmospheric reentry, probably that of a meteorite.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon with two white headlights
description: On March 17, 1997, around 8:00 AM, several witnesses and aircraft crews observed the passage of a green rocket whose downward trajectory and descriptions suggested atmospheric reentry or the reentry of space debris. Later that same day, around 8:30 PM, a market gardener observed a luminous phenomenon composed of two white lights. Attempting to illuminate this phenomenon with his lamp, the witness observed the white lights go out. They were replaced by a light shone directly at him, as if observing him. When this light went out, the other two lights came back on. Then, tilting to one side, an object gained some altitude and departed at a rapid pace. The entire observation lasted 5 to 7 minutes. No noise was noted. Another witness reported, at the same time, the relatively slow passage of an elongated orange luminous phenomenon. For this second observation, none of the crews flying in the area at that time noticed anything. Both observations were the subject of a joint summary report. This second phenomenon remains unexplained.

summary: Observation of an egg-shaped creature. Hoax
description: On January 14, 1997, around 5:00 PM, a witness out jogging reported encountering an ovoid being surmounted by a triangular head. This being allegedly fled upon his approach, dropping a soft, reddish-brown object which the witness picked up and which he claimed had remained in his pocket. The witness then presented this object as an "extraterrestrial artifact." The investigation quickly revealed this to be a fabrication.
